scripts.opening:opening:
[intrigued] JAUNT: THE MERCHANT AND MRS. CATON. [short pause] Monday morning... 21 November 1904. A telegram has come from New York, [softly] and the blinds are down in a house on Calumet Avenue.

Four stops, on foot, from the widow's door, through the back yards the servants share, to the front steps of Marshall Field, the merchant prince of Chicago. [conspiratorially] Everybody on Prairie Avenue knows this story. [whispers] Nobody says it out loud. Thirty years of dinners, voyages and rumours are about to come to an end, [short pause] and this morning the only people talking are the ones who carry the coal.

[short pause] [quietly] Start at Calumet Avenue, at the house with the drawn blinds.
scripts.stop:widow: [quietly] Calumet Avenue, behind Prairie, at the side of the Caton house. Its blinds are drawn. On Friday Arthur J. Caton died at New York's Waldorf-Astoria hotel, [short pause] and nobody can quite say of what. "Some said he succumbed to liver failure. Others ascribed the demise to peritonitis." [lowering voice] A newspaper downstate will hint that he took his own life. He was a judge's son, a lawyer who loved golf and polo and bred horses and dogs on the family farm. His wife Delia, a hardware heiress he married in 1876, [warmly] gave the best parties in town: Arthur Meeker's mother "always declared that nobody ever gave such wonderful parties as Delia Caton". [short pause] There were no children. [softly] This morning... there is a widow, and in the side yard the news is going from the house to the stable. [short pause] Go round the back, to the yards between Calumet and Prairie.
scripts.stop:yards: [conspiratorially] The back yards, where Calumet meets Prairie at the rear fence. [short pause] Turn round... and the Field house is right there, its coach house on the alley. The servants of the two houses have shared this ground for years, and they have heard the talk. Arthur Meeker, who grew up on this street, wrote it down: [whispers] "it was even absurdly asserted that an underground tunnel connected the Caton house on Calumet with the Field house on Prairie, which was just in front of it, or just back." [amused] Meeker called it absurd, and it was. [short pause] But a society diarist recorded that "Delia sometimes traveled to Europe with Marshall Field without Arthur accompanying them." [long pause] [quietly] Now Arthur is dead, Field's wife has been dead eight years, and a laundress from the Field house is leaning on the fence. Walk on to Prairie Avenue and find the man himself.
scripts.stop:field: [measured] 1905 Prairie, the Marshall Field house: built in 1876 for some $2 million, "the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity". Field is the richest merchant in the city. [amused] Years ago he proposed to his first wife by jumping aboard her train as it left Chicago; [wryly] one account says that "Mrs. Field led Marshall Field a hell-on-earth life", [softly] and Nannie Field died in France in 1896. [short pause] Meeker put the rest plainly: "he fell in love with his friend's wife years before he was able to marry her." And: "In the Nineties, divorce was unthinkable: they had to wait for him (Arthur Caton) to die, which, distressingly, he didn't do until 1904." [long pause] [quietly] That was Friday. Thomas Benson, the butler, has the door; John Dunford, the coachman, comes round from the stable. [short pause] The house will be razed in 1955.
scripts.stop:talk: [warmly] From up the street the Field house looks like any other on the row. It is not. Field never liked making speeches, and one night at one of the Catons' grand dinners he was called on to say a few words. [amused] Delia sprang to her feet and spoke for him: "Mr. Field just wants me to remind you that the White Sale starts next Monday." [laughs] It was a joke about his store, made by another man's wife, at her husband's table, and the guests who told it afterwards told it as the night everybody saw how close those two were. [short pause] [conspiratorially] The ladies passing the Field house this morning are not looking at it, and they are talking about nothing else. [short pause] [softly] Arthur Caton is not yet buried. Everyone can guess what happens next, [whispers] and nobody can say it.
scripts.ending:london: [softly] End of the walk. [short pause] They waited less than a year. In 1905 they married in London, at St. Margaret's, Westminster; the licence gave Delia as 46 and Field as 70. [tenderly] "The ceremony was quiet, and attended only by a few friends." They came home to Chicago as man and wife, [short pause] [sadly] and in January 1906... Marshall Field was dead of pneumonia, caught on a New Year's golf course with Robert Todd Lincoln. [long pause] After thirty years of waiting... they had a few months. [short pause] Delia got $1 million and the house, moved to Washington, where her mansion was called the Pink Palace, and lived until 1937.
